newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: FEATURE - Turkmenistan: a weird union of poverty and luxury.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Turkmenistan: a weird union of poverty and luxury.

text.p: Glitzy hotels, casinos and restaurants are mushrooming in the Turkmen capital. But ordinary Turkmens, cast into poverty, seem oblivious to the screaming luxury and many sell family heirlooms to survive.
The main offerings, displayed at a flea market on the outskirts of the capital Ashgabat, are Turkmenistan's traditional richly ornamented hand-woven carpets.
The older they get, the sleeker and silkier they look.
"No, I do not regret selling these carpets. But I feel sorry for my kids left at home, who have nothing to eat," said one carpet seller, a weary-looking man in his 30s.
A 100-year-old carpet can be bought on this market for around $200, but there are many more sellers than buyers.

Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov, who enjoys a Soviet-era personality cult and goes under the official title of Turkmenbashi, or "head of Turkmens", has banned exports of old carpets, and sellers can no longer count on a stream of rich foreigners, their clients in the past.
"Why am I here? Maybe, it is against the policy of our great leader but I just need money," said a middle-aged woman.
She said she had more antique carpets at home, but seemed afraid at the thought that one day she would sell the last one.
SELLING TO MAKE ENDS MEET

For many, selling carpets and other family heirlooms is simply a way to make ends meet. Salaries, paid in manat banknotes adorned with Niyazov's picture, average just $16 a month in this desert country of 4.5 million.

But Turkmens, the proud descendants of Turkic nomads, are reluctant to talk of their hardships or give their names -- their great leader Turkmenbashi is watching from posters on each street corner and portraits on facades of houses.
"We should glorify our motherland," says a Niyazov quote emblazoned in golden letters outside the new and ultra-modern Ashgabat International Airport, named after Turkmenbashi.
"Glorification" includes a luxury Turkmenbashi shopping mall along the main thoroughfare and a line of 30 four and five-star hotels stretching for several kilometres (miles) on the city's edge.
But shops are half-empty after a dismal grain harvest and most of the hotels have few guests.
Residents near the hotel cluster see few benefits from the building boom -- their water supplies are switched off regularly while the hotels change the water in their swimming pools.
"NOISY" NIGHTLIFE CURBED
Police drive customers from restaurants and casinos after 11 p.m., in line with a Niyazov order issued after a group of Muslim clergy complained about "noisy night life".
But there is remarkably little organised opposition, despite the hardships of everyday life.
Last year, there might have been riots after Turkmenistan gathered a meagre 400,000 tonnes of grain instead of 1.2 million tonnes initially targeted.
But Niyazov, the country's communist boss in the past, introduced a system of cheap bread rations, tested by communists for decades.
"The general impression is that people are too worn out by working out how to get their daily bread and they pay little attention to Niyazov's personality cult," said a local reporter.
SOME REFORMS UNDERTAKEN
Niyazov has taken some small steps to reform the farm sector, freeing agricultural producers from value-added and profit taxes and giving some farmers the right to own land.
He has also tripled the domestic price of grain from next year's harvest, bringing it to 400,000 manats ($97) per tonne. The world market price is around $140 a tonne.
But Turkmenistan's future wealth lies in exploiting its huge reserves of oil and natural gas and international companies are already renting spacious offices in Ashgabat.
Turkmen officials talk seriously of a "miracle in the making".
"Now they are all laughing at our poverty and stigmatising us for our personality cult," a Foreign Ministry official told Reuters.
"But all this criticism and the haughty attitude to our national characteristics will stop when Turkmenistan becomes the second Kuwait or Saudi Arabia thanks to its natural reserves."
